title: Inserting and Finding Documents
summary: Create documents with insertOne and insertMany, read them back with find and findOne, shape results with projections, and sort, limit and count them.
introduction: Create and Read are the two halves of CRUD you use most, and in MongoDB they are four methods: insertOne, insertMany, find and findOne. This lesson builds the product catalogue that the rest of the tutorial queries, then reads it back in every way an application needs: filtered, projected to a few fields, sorted, limited to a page and counted. Along the way you learn what a cursor is and what the shell is really doing when it prints results.
learningObjectives: Insert one or many documents and read the result the server returns
Filter documents with find and findOne and choose fields with a projection
Sort, limit, skip and count results, and iterate a cursor

blocks.text: `insertOne` takes a document; `insertMany` takes an array of documents and sends them in one round trip, which is much faster than inserting in a loop. Start with a clean `products` collection so that your results match the outputs below. Explicit numeric `_id` values keep the examples predictable; in real applications you usually let MongoDB generate an `ObjectId`, as shown at the end of the lesson.

blocks.code:
use shop
db.products.drop()
db.products.insertMany([
  { _id: 1, name: 'Mechanical keyboard', price: 89.5, category: 'peripherals', stock: 12, tags: ['usb', 'backlit'], rating: 4.6 },
  { _id: 2, name: 'Wireless mouse', price: 24.99, category: 'peripherals', stock: 0, tags: ['wireless', 'usb'], rating: 4.1 },
  { _id: 3, name: '27-inch monitor', price: 219, category: 'displays', stock: 5, tags: ['4k', 'hdmi'], rating: 4.8 },
  { _id: 4, name: 'Desk lamp', price: 24.5, category: 'office', stock: 40, tags: ['led'] },
  { _id: 5, name: 'USB-C hub', price: 39, category: 'peripherals', stock: 8, tags: ['usb'], rating: 3.9 },
  { _id: 6, name: 'Webcam', price: 59, category: 'peripherals', stock: 3, tags: ['usb', 'video'], rating: 4.3, discontinued: true }
])

blocks.text: `drop()` returns `true` when the collection existed (and `false` when it did not). The insert result lists the `_id` of every new document by its position in the array. Notice that the lamp has no `rating` and only the webcam has `discontinued`: documents in one collection do not need identical fields, and the next lesson shows how to query for that.

By default `insertMany` is **ordered**: documents are written in array order and the operation stops at the first failure, leaving the earlier documents in place. Pass `{ ordered: false }` to insert everything that can be inserted and report the failures afterwards. Each document is written atomically, but a multi-document insert as a whole is not; the [Transactions](/tutorials/mongodb/transactions) lesson covers all-or-nothing writes.

`find(filter, projection)` returns every document matching the filter; `findOne` returns the first match or `null`. A filter is a document whose fields must equal the given values. A **projection** chooses which fields come back: `1` includes a field and `0` excludes it. `_id` is always included unless you exclude it explicitly, and sending fewer fields over the network is one of the cheapest optimisations there is.

blocks.content:
{
  _id: 2,
  name: 'Wireless mouse',
  price: 24.99,
  category: 'peripherals',
  stock: 0,
  tags: [ 'wireless', 'usb' ],
  rating: 4.1
}
null

blocks.text: A `findOne` with no match returns `null` rather than throwing, so application code must check for it. A `find` with no match prints nothing at all in mongosh and yields an empty array in a driver. An empty filter, `find({})` or simply `find()`, matches every document.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Types are part of the match. `find({ price: '219' })` returns nothing, because the stored price is the number `219` and the filter has the string `'219'`. The same applies to ids: `find({ _id: '3' })` does not find `_id: 3`, and a string copied from a URL does not match an `ObjectId` until you wrap it in `ObjectId(...)`.

Without a sort, documents come back in *natural order*, which is usually insertion order but is not guaranteed and can change after updates. Whenever order matters, say so with `sort`, where `1` is ascending and `-1` descending. `limit` caps the number of results and `skip` jumps past the first ones, which together give you paging:

blocks.code:
db.products.find({}, { _id: 0, name: 1, price: 1 }).sort({ price: -1 }).limit(2)
db.products.countDocuments({ category: 'peripherals' })

blocks.text: `countDocuments(filter)` counts exactly, scanning whatever the filter needs. `estimatedDocumentCount()` returns the collection's metadata count instantly, with no filter, which is ideal for dashboards where an approximation is fine.

`find` does not return documents; it returns a **cursor**, an object that fetches documents from the server in batches as you consume them. That is why `sort`, `limit` and `skip` chain after `find`: they configure the cursor before the first batch is requested. mongosh automatically iterates a cursor you do not assign and prints the first 20 documents; type `it` to see the next 20. In code, you iterate explicitly:

blocks.content:
Desk lamp: 24.5
Wireless mouse: 24.99
USB-C hub: 39
Webcam: 59
Mechanical keyboard: 89.5
27-inch monitor: 219

blocks.text: `toArray()` pulls every remaining document into memory, which is convenient for small result sets and dangerous for large ones. In the Node.js driver the same cursor supports `for await` loops, as the [Node.js driver](/tutorials/mongodb/node-driver) lesson shows.
Leave out `_id` and the shell generates an `ObjectId` before sending the document. The result tells you which value was used; yours will differ from the one shown here.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Page through the catalogue two products at a time with `.sort({ name: 1 }).skip(2).limit(2)`, then change the skip to 4. Then count how many products cost less than 50 by combining `countDocuments` with the `$lt` operator from the next lesson.

questions.question: What does `db.products.findOne({ name: 'Nothing' })` return when no document matches?
questions.explanation: `findOne` returns `null` when nothing matches. It never throws for a missing document, so application code has to check the result.

questions.question: The projection `{ name: 1, price: 1 }` returns only the `name` and `price` fields.
questions.explanation: `_id` is included by default even when the projection does not mention it. Add `_id: 0` to leave it out.

seo.title: MongoDB insertOne, insertMany, find and findOne
seo.description: Insert documents with insertOne and insertMany, query them with find and findOne, use projections, sort, limit, skip and countDocuments, and understand cursors.
